interactions.label: Sucralfate can be safely combined with a proton pump inhibitor because both drug

params.question: Sucralfate can be safely combined with a proton pump inhibitor because both drugs reduce gastric acid secretion.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Incorrect. Sucralfate does not reduce acid secretion at all — it is a mucosal protectant that forms a physical barrier over ulcerated tissue. It needs an acidic environment (pH below 4) to polymerise, so a PPI, which raises gastric pH, defeats its mechanism of action.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Sucralfate is a mucosal protectant, not an acid suppressant — it sits on the opposite pillar of APD pharmacotherapy. It requires an acidic gastric pH to polymerise into its protective gel, so combining it with a PPI, which raises pH, prevents sucralfate from activating.

interactions.label: A 70-year-old patient with Parkinson's disease develops gastroparesis. Metoclopr

params.question: A 70-year-old patient with Parkinson's disease develops gastroparesis. Metoclopramide is considered but poses a specific risk. Which receptor interaction explains why metoclopramide can worsen parkinsonian symptoms?

answers.text: Agonism at 5-HT₄ receptors in the substantia nigra

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Metoclopramide's 5-HT₄ agonism acts on the myenteric plexus to promote gastric motility — it does not have a significant central 5-HT₄ effect that would impair movement.

answers.text: Antagonism at D₂ receptors in the basal ganglia after crossing the blood–brain barrier

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Metoclopramide crosses the blood–brain barrier and blocks central D₂ receptors, reducing dopaminergic transmission in the basal ganglia — the same pathway already impaired in Parkinson's disease.

answers.text: Blockade of muscarinic receptors in the extrapyramidal system

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Anticholinergic agents actually help parkinsonian symptoms by restoring the dopamine–acetylcholine balance. Metoclopramide does not block muscarinic receptors; its central adverse effect is via D₂ antagonism.

answers.text: Agonism at H₁ receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: H₁ receptor agonism is not part of metoclopramide's pharmacology. Antihistamines (H₁ antagonists) are used for motion sickness, not for gastroparesis.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the receptor-based classification. Metoclopramide has two key actions: 5-HT₄ agonism in the gut (prokinetic) and D₂ antagonism centrally (antiemetic). The central D₂ blockade is what worsens Parkinson's motor symptoms.

Well done. Mapping each antiemetic to its receptor target is essential — metoclopramide's D₂ antagonism is therapeutic at the CTZ but harmful in the basal ganglia of a patient with Parkinson's disease.

interactions.label: Which class of laxatives is considered the safest option for long-term use in ch

params.question: Which class of laxatives is considered the safest option for long-term use in chronic constipation, provided the patient maintains adequate fluid intake?

answers.text: Stimulant laxatives such as senna and bisacodyl

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Stimulant laxatives trigger colonic contractions directly and are meant for short courses only. Long-term use can lead to dependence and electrolyte disturbances.

Magnesium hydroxide acts fast but carries a risk of hypermagnesaemia in patients with renal impairment. Polyethylene glycol is a safer osmotic option for chronic use, but bulk-forming agents remain first-line.
Liquid paraffin carries significant long-term risks including lipoid pneumonia from aspiration and impaired absorption of fat-soluble vitamins. It is no longer recommended for chronic use.

answers.text: Bulk-forming agents such as ispaghula and methylcellulose

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Bulk-forming agents absorb water, swell, and stimulate peristalsis naturally — mimicking the physiological mechanism. They must be taken with plenty of water to avoid intestinal obstruction.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the five-class laxative taxonomy. Bulk-forming agents (ispaghula, methylcellulose) are the safest long-term option because they mimic natural fibre. The key precaution is adequate water intake to prevent obstruction.
Exactly right. Bulk-forming agents work by the most physiological mechanism and have the best long-term safety profile, making them first-line for chronic constipation.

interactions.label: A junior doctor prescribes azathioprine to a patient diagnosed with irritable bo

params.question: A junior doctor prescribes azathioprine to a patient diagnosed with irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhoea (IBS-D). What is the primary reason this is a dangerous prescribing error?

answers.text: Azathioprine accelerates gut motility and worsens diarrhoea in IBS

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Azathioprine does not directly affect gut motility. Its danger in IBS is not about worsening symptoms but about exposing the patient to immunosuppression without any therapeutic benefit.

answers.text: IBS is a functional disorder that does not require immunomodulation, so the patient is exposed to serious immunosuppressive risks without benefit

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. IBS is a functional disorder — there is no mucosal inflammation or immune dysregulation to treat. Azathioprine's bone marrow suppression, hepatotoxicity, and infection risk are unjustifiable in this setting.

answers.text: Azathioprine is only effective when combined with a biologic agent and cannot be used as monotherapy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Azathioprine can be used as monotherapy for maintaining remission in IBD. The issue here is that IBS does not warrant immunomodulation at all — the wrong disease, not the wrong drug combination.

answers.text: IBS-D patients have an exaggerated immune response that makes azathioprine's immunosuppression dangerously excessive

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: IBS is not an immune-mediated disease. There is no exaggerated immune response to suppress. The correct IBS-D agents — loperamide, low-dose amitriptyline, or rifaximin — target motility, visceral sensation, or gut flora.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the IBD vs IBS drug divide. IBD drugs (aminosalicylates, corticosteroids, immunomodulators, biologics, JAK inhibitors) target inflammation. IBS drugs (loperamide, amitriptyline, linaclotide, mebeverine) target symptoms. Never cross these two lists.

Well done. The single most important distinction in GI pharmacotherapy is keeping IBD drugs (anti-inflammatory, immunomodulatory) completely separate from IBS drugs (symptom-targeted, non-immune-modulating).

interactions.label: In a patient with H. pylori-positive duodenal ulcer disease, which therapeutic s

params.question: In a patient with H. pylori-positive duodenal ulcer disease, which therapeutic step is the single most important factor in preventing ulcer relapse?

answers.text: Maintaining intragastric pH above 6 continuously with high-dose PPI therapy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Raising pH above 6 supports haemostasis in a bleeding ulcer, but it is not the key factor in preventing long-term relapse. Without addressing the underlying infection, acid suppression alone allows recurrence once therapy stops.

answers.text: Healing the mucosal lesion endoscopically within four to eight weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Confirming mucosal healing is important, but if the underlying H. pylori infection persists, the ulcer is very likely to recur after acid suppression is withdrawn.

answers.text: Eradicating Helicobacter pylori with appropriate combination therapy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. H. pylori eradication is the single most important factor in preventing ulcer relapse. Without it, relapse rates exceed 80 per cent within a year, even after successful initial healing.

answers.text: Stopping all NSAIDs and advising complete smoking cessation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Removing aggravating factors like NSAIDs and smoking is essential, but in an H. pylori-positive patient, eradicating the organism itself is the most critical step to prevent recurrence.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recall the five-step therapeutic hierarchy: symptom relief → mucosal healing → H. pylori eradication → remove aggravating factors → prevent complications. Eradication is the single most important step for preventing relapse.
Exactly right. H. pylori eradication transforms peptic ulcer disease from a chronic relapsing condition into a curable one — it is the cornerstone of the treatment hierarchy.
